strengths: Addresses an important and comparatively under-explored problem—synthetic survival data generation—and proposes the first diffusion-based method for it, which is a meaningful conceptual step beyond the GAN-based SurvivalGAN.

The method is well-motivated: an end-to-end model that jointly generates mixed-type covariates, event times, and the censoring indicator using masked + variance-exploding diffusion with a Cox-based survival loss and adaptive λ_surv scaling.

Broad and reasonably rigorous empirical setup: three medical datasets, five baselines (including the survival-specific SurvivalGAN and the tabular-diffusion TabDiff), five downstream survival models, ten seeds, and multiple metric families (JS/Wasserstein covariate fidelity, TSTR C-index/Brier, RMST gap/KM MSE), plus a downsampling sensitivity study.

Strong and consistent covariate-fidelity gains: SurvDiff attains the best JS distance on all three datasets (e.g., METABRIC 0.0048 vs TabDiff 0.0266) and better downstream C-index/Brier on AIDS and GBSG2, with a clear margin over SurvivalGAN.
Reproducibility is comparatively good: dataset descriptions, full hyperparameter tables, architecture, sampling steps, and training schedules are provided.
weaknesses: The central survival loss in Eq. (10) is written incorrectly: the denominator sums exp(r_i) rather than exp(r_j) over the risk set R(t_i). This error sits in the paper's core objective and needs correction/clarification.

The headline claim of 'preserving censoring mechanisms' is never directly evaluated. No metric compares the censoring distribution or censoring rate between real and synthetic data, even though censoring preservation is one of the two stated desiderata.

Against the strongest and most relevant baseline (TabDiff), results are mixed, and on the survival-specific metrics in Table 7 TabDiff often matches or beats SurvDiff (e.g., AIDS RMST 0.0066 vs 0.0134; GBSG2 KM MSE 0.0005 vs 0.0062; METABRIC RMST 0.0048 vs 0.0268). This undercuts the claim that the survival-tailored loss is what yields faithful event-time distributions.

No ablation isolates the contributions of the survival loss, the sparsity-aware weighting, or the adaptive λ_surv. Since the largest gains appear in covariate fidelity—something the survival loss is not designed to improve—it is unclear whether improvements stem from the survival objective or from other architectural/training differences; this is unexplained.

The sparsity-aware weighting (Eq. 11) exponentially downweights late events; the stated rationale (stability from small risk sets) is in tension with the goal of reproducing long-term event-time distributions, and it is neither ablated nor empirically justified.

Statistical significance is not assessed, and several claimed 'large improvements' have heavily overlapping standard deviations (e.g., AIDS C-index 0.6826 ± 0.0541 vs SurvivalGAN 0.6361 ± 0.0594), so the improvements may be within noise.

Presentation problems: the Eq. (10) error, a broken cross-reference ('Figure 4.3'), inconsistent capitalization (SURVDIFF vs SurvDiff), a garbled Table 1 layout, and typos ('re-producing', 'Wegrebe'). There is also no explicit limitations section and no discussion of privacy considerations, which is notable for synthetic health data.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely understudied and clinically relevant problem: synthetic survival data generation, where covariates, event times, and right-censoring must be jointly modeled.

The overall design is reasonable and well-motivated: extending a strong mixed-type tabular diffusion backbone (TabDiff) with a survival-aware objective and masked/VE noise processes for discrete and continuous variables.

The experimental protocol is fairly comprehensive for the claim: three medical datasets (AIDS, GBSG2, METABRIC), five baselines, five downstream survival models, and results averaged over 10 seeds with standard deviations.
Covariate fidelity results (JS distance) are strong and consistent across all three datasets, and the small-sample sensitivity study (Table 8) is a useful addition.
Reproducibility is partially supported: architecture, schedules, and hyperparameters for SurvDiff and all baselines are tabulated in the supplement.
weaknesses: The central claim is not supported by the paper's own survival-specific metrics. In Table 7, generic TabDiff (which has no survival loss) achieves clearly better RMST gap on AIDS (0.0066 vs 0.0134) and METABRIC (0.0048 vs 0.0268), and SurvivalGAN achieves lower KM MSE on AIDS (0.0002 vs 0.0003) and METABRIC (0.0124 vs 0.0029). Since the paper's stated purpose is to '(i) reproduce realistic event-time distributions and (ii) preserve censoring mechanisms,' the evidence contradicts rather than supports the core selling point of the survival loss.

Novelty is limited. The masking diffusion, VE SDE, noise schedules, and transformer/MLP architecture are taken directly from TabDiff (Shi et al., 2024b); the only substantive addition is a Cox partial-likelihood term with an ad-hoc exponential decay weighting. This is a fairly incremental delta over an existing tabular diffusion model.

'Preserving the censoring mechanism' is oversold. Censoring is modeled only as a binary indicator E fed through the same masked-diffusion channel as any discrete covariate; there is no explicit modeling of the censoring-time distribution. TabDiff handles E the same way, so the claim of a survival-tailored censoring treatment is not substantiated.

Equation 10 contains a subscript error: the denominator writes exp(r_i) over the risk set instead of exp(r_j), which is incorrect for the Cox partial likelihood. Given this is the paper's central objective, the error is concerning for reproducibility.

The survival loss is under-specified. It is unclear at which diffusion noise level the survival head is applied, whether risk scores come from denoised x_0 estimates at sampled u, and how noisy intermediate predictions interact with risk sets derived from observed event times. This ambiguity is important because it determines whether the loss genuinely shapes the generative distribution of T and E.

The sparsity-aware weighting (Eq. 11) introduces hyperparameters τ and α that are neither reported nor ablated, and downweighting late events plausibly biases the generated survival tail — the opposite of the fidelity goal — without any empirical validation.

No privacy evaluation is provided, despite the clinical framing ('train downstream survival models without direct access to patient-level data'). For synthetic clinical data, distance-to-closest-record or membership-inference metrics are essential and their absence is a material gap.

There is no limitations section; the Discussion is promotional (clinical considerations only) and does not acknowledge any of the above issues. The paper also overclaims throughout ('consistently outperforms,' 'first,' 'preserves censoring mechanisms').

Presentation issues: the overview references a non-existent 'Figure 4.3'; JS values in the t-SNE figure captions do not match Table 2; Table 1 is poorly formatted; and several downstream improvements fall within one standard deviation of baselines (e.g., GBSG2 C-index 0.6453 ± 0.0201 vs SurvivalGAN 0.6396 ± 0.0168), so 'large improvements' is overstated.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: synthetic survival data generation is underexplored, and the paper correctly identifies that generic tabular generators ignore time-to-event and censoring structure. The task framing (covariate fidelity + downstream survival performance) is sensible.

Reasonable methodological contribution: SURVDIFF is an end-to-end masked+Gaussian diffusion model that jointly generates mixed-type covariates, event indicator, and event time. Combining TabDiff-style mixed-type diffusion with a survival-tailored auxiliary loss is a plausible and clean design, and it is the first diffusion model explicitly aimed at synthetic survival data.

Solid empirical protocol: three real medical datasets (AIDS, GBSG2, METABRIC), five generative baselines including the closest prior work (SurvivalGAN) and the most relevant ablation (TabDiff), six metrics (JS, Wasserstein, C-index, Brier, RMST gap, KM MSE), and 10 seeds with mean±s.d. reported. Hyperparameters for all models are given in the supplement, aiding reproducibility.

The results are largely positive where they matter most: covariate fidelity (JS) improves across all datasets, and downstream C-index/Brier improve over SurvivalGAN, with the gains largest under heavy censoring (AIDS, GBSG2). The small-sample downsampling study (Table 8) is a practically relevant addition.
The paper is generally honest about mixed results (e.g., 'comparable performance' on survival metrics in Supplement D, ties with TabDiff on METABRIC), which is a point in its favor.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'preserving the censoring mechanism' is not supported by the method as described. The survival loss (Eq. 10) is essentially the standard Cox partial likelihood with a heuristic decay weighting applied to risk scores derived from denoised covariates; it does not model the conditional censoring distribution p(C | X, T). The censoring indicator E is simply generated as another discrete variable via masked diffusion, which captures its joint/marginal distribution but does not constitute an explicit mechanism for preserving censoring. The paper repeatedly conflates 'accounting for censoring during training' (censored points in the risk set) with 'reproducing the censoring mechanism' (generating faithful conditional censoring).

No censoring-specific evaluation is provided. Given that censoring preservation is a headline claim, one would expect a direct metric (e.g., fidelity of the conditional distribution of E given X and T, or a comparison of estimated censoring distributions/KM of censoring). Instead only covariate fidelity, downstream survival metrics, and marginal KM/RMST are reported, none of which isolate the censoring mechanism.

Technical issues in the loss. Eq. (10) writes the denominator as sum_j exp(r_i) rather than exp(r_j), which is a clear typo but makes the objective ambiguous as written. The sparsity-aware weighting (Eq. 11) changes the estimand (it is no longer the Cox partial likelihood) and its justification ('small risk sets cause unstable gradients') is asserted rather than demonstrated; moreover tau and alpha are not reported in the hyperparameter table (Table 4), harming reproducibility of a core component.

Unclear metric definitions. Wasserstein distance for mixed continuous/discrete/mixed-type data and the exact JS distance computation are not specified, and the reported magnitudes (e.g., WS ~0.03) suggest normalization that is never explained. Without this, the fidelity comparisons are hard to interpret or reproduce.

Baselines are not all equally appropriate. NFlow/TVAE/CTGAN do not model survival structure at all, so outperforming them on survival metrics is expected; the informative comparisons are against SurvivalGAN and TabDiff, where the picture is more mixed (TabDiff is better or tied on METABRIC Wasserstein, KM MSE, and RMST gap in Tables 2/7). The claim that SURVDIFF 'consistently outperforms' overstates the evidence for METABRIC.

Several reported differences are within noise (e.g., METABRIC C-index 0.6117 ± 0.0111 vs TabDiff 0.6118 ± 0.0095), yet the narrative emphasizes consistent superiority. No significance testing is reported despite 10 seeds.

Code availability is not mentioned, which is important for a synthetic-data-generation method; the ablation isolating the survival loss (e.g., diffusion-only vs diffusion+survival loss vs diffusion+unweighted Cox) is not run, so the marginal value of the proposed loss and weighting is not directly established.
